newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa recovering, wants to go home.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa recovering, wants to go home.

text.p: Mother Teresa was recovering from heart trouble in a Calcutta nursing home on Saturday and told doctors she wanted to go home.
The 86-year-old Roman Catholic missionary was taken to hospital with an irregular heart beat on Friday, the third time since August she had been admitted for emergency care.
"She is quite cheerful and she wants to go home," Dinamani Banerjee, a member of the medical board looking after her at the Woodlands Nursing Home in the eastern Indian city, told Reuters.
"She is responding well to the treatment. But we want to keep her under observation for a few more days," he said.
"We (medical board members) are meeting tomorrow to take a decision on her release," he added.
Earlier, Mother Teresa, known as the "Saint of the Gutters" for her work with the poor and destitute, said morning prayers in an intensive care unit, her doctor said.
"As of now she is doing well," the doctor, S.K. Sen, medical director of Woodlands, told reporters.
"She is responding very well to the treatment. She is breathing normally," he added. Her heart rate was being controlled but would take time before becoming normal.
The hospital issued a medical bulletin saying the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner, fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989, was gradually improving. "She is alert and cheeful," it said.
Mother Teresa spoke to some nuns from her Missionaries of Charity religious order in her hospital room.
Mother Teresa has spent time in hospital for heart disease, bacterial pneumonia, broken ribs, malaria, and lung problems.
She spent nearly three weeks at Woodlands in August and September for heart trouble, malaria and pneumonia.
Two weeks after returning to her Calcutta-based order, she fell off a chair and hit her head. A brain scan revealed a blood clot in the brain. She was released after it disappeared.
Last Saturday, Mother Teresa received honorary American citizenship, one of only five people in U.S. history, in a ceremony led by U.S. Ambassador to India Frank Wisner.
She began her life's work in the slums of Calcutta, India's most densely populated city, in 1949.
